Now part 3: Drop Gaussian assumptions; retain only independence, zero means, variances τ², σ². Then conditional expectation E[R|S=s] is not determined by covariance alone except via linear projection: the best linear predictor is Cov(R,S)/Var(S) s = τ²/(τ²+σ²) s = ρ s. But E[R|S=s] generally ≠ ρ s; also Var(R|S=s) is not constant w = τ²σ²/(τ²+σ²); indeed the conditional variance can depend on s and can even be zero in some regions (e.g., degenerate conditional distributions). Also E[Y|S=s] = a E[R|S=s] - k|a| still holds by linearity of expectation (cost deterministic), but the no-trade region |ρ s| ≤ k is no longer valid. Also the Gaussian-specific quadratic J formula fails.

Given S = s = τ + σ, R = τ with probability 1 (since only one pair gives that sum, assuming τ ≠ σ... need to consider multiplicities). E.g., τ = 12, σ = 16: S values: 28, -4, 4, -28. Contradiction: both the magnitude and the risk term wrong. Great counterexample.
